concepts.description_formal: For a function f and a point a, the instantaneous rate of change at a is the limit of the average rates of change of f over intervals containing a as the length of those intervals tends to zero.
concepts.description_plain: An instantaneous rate is what average rates settle towards as the interval shrinks to nothing.
concepts.name: Instantaneous rate of change as a limit of average rates
concepts.notation: average rate of change; instantaneous rate of change

concepts.description_formal: The limit of f(x) as x approaches c is the real number R if f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to R by taking x sufficiently close to c and not equal to c.
concepts.description_plain: A limit is the single value the outputs crowd around as the inputs approach a target, whether or not the function is defined there.
concepts.name: The limit of a function at a point
concepts.notation: lim as x approaches c of f(x) equals R

concepts.description_formal: Analytic limit notation names the independent variable, the target value, the direction of approach when one sided, and the value claimed for the limit.
concepts.description_plain: The symbols for a limit, including the one sided arrows, say precisely which approach is meant.
concepts.name: Limit notation and its reading
concepts.notation: lim as x approaches c from the left; lim as x approaches c from the right

concepts.description_formal: The two sided limit of f at c exists and equals R if and only if both one sided limits at c exist and equal R.
concepts.description_plain: A two sided limit exists only when the approach from the left and the approach from the right give the same value.
concepts.name: One sided limits and two sided existence
concepts.notation: left hand limit; right hand limit

concepts.description_formal: The limit of f at c fails to exist if the one sided limits differ, if f is unbounded near c, or if f oscillates without settling near c.
concepts.description_plain: A limit can fail because the sides disagree, because the values grow without bound, or because the values keep oscillating.
concepts.name: Ways a limit can fail to exist

concepts.description_formal: Graphical and numerical information supports an estimate of a limit; the scale of a graph and the spacing of a table can conceal behaviour that changes the estimate.
concepts.description_plain: A graph or a short table can suggest a limit value but cannot prove one.
concepts.name: Estimation of a limit from a graph or a table

concepts.description_formal: If the limits of f and g at c exist, the limit of a sum, difference, product, or constant multiple is the corresponding combination of the limits, and the same holds for a quotient when the limit of the denominator is not zero.
concepts.description_plain: Limits pass through sums, differences, products, quotients, and compositions when the pieces have limits.
concepts.name: Limit theorems for combinations of functions

concepts.description_formal: An expression whose numerator and denominator both tend to zero carries no value by substitution; an equivalent expression valid near but not at the point determines the limit.
concepts.description_plain: When substitution gives zero over zero the expression must be rewritten before the limit can be read off.
concepts.name: Indeterminate form handled by rewriting

concepts.description_formal: Classifying a limit expression by its behaviour under substitution, as a determinate value, an indeterminate form, or an unbounded quotient, selects the procedure that resolves it.
concepts.description_plain: The form the expression takes under substitution decides which method to use.
concepts.name: Selection of a procedure for a limit

concepts.description_formal: If g(x) is less than or equal to f(x) and f(x) is less than or equal to h(x) for all x near c except possibly at c, and the limits of g and h at c are both L, then the limit of f at c is L.
concepts.description_plain: If a function is trapped between two functions that meet at a value, it meets them there too.
concepts.name: The squeeze theorem

concepts.description_formal: A limit claim expressed in one representation has an equivalent expression in each other representation, and conversion between them preserves the claim.
concepts.description_plain: The same limit fact can be shown by a graph, a table, a formula, or a sentence, and these must agree.
concepts.name: Connecting graphical, numerical, analytical, and verbal limit statements

concepts.description_formal: A discontinuity at c is removable when the limit at c exists but does not equal f(c) or f(c) is undefined, a jump when the one sided limits exist and differ, and an infinite discontinuity when a one sided limit is infinite.
concepts.description_plain: A break in a graph is removable, a jump, or an infinite break at a vertical asymptote.
concepts.name: Classification of discontinuities

concepts.description_formal: A function f is continuous at x equals c provided that f(c) exists, the limit of f(x) as x approaches c exists, and that limit equals f(c).
concepts.description_plain: Continuity at a point needs the function value, the limit, and their agreement.
concepts.name: Continuity at a point as three conditions

concepts.description_formal: Continuity on an interval is continuity at each point of the interval; polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous at every point of their domains.
concepts.description_plain: A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every point of that interval.
concepts.name: Continuity on an interval

concepts.description_formal: If the limit exists at a discontinuity it can be removed by defining or redefining f at that point as the limit; for a piecewise function continuity at a boundary requires the two branch expressions and the function value to agree there.
concepts.description_plain: A removable break can be repaired by defining the value to equal the limit, and a piecewise rule is made continuous by matching the two branch values at a boundary.
concepts.name: Removing a discontinuity and matching a piecewise function

concepts.description_formal: The limit of f at c is infinite when f(x) increases or decreases without bound as x approaches c; such behaviour on either side gives a vertical asymptote at x equals c.
concepts.description_plain: Values that grow without bound near an input mark a vertical asymptote there.
concepts.name: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes

concepts.description_formal: The limit of f(x) as x increases or decreases without bound describes the end behaviour of f, and a finite such limit L gives the horizontal asymptote y equals L.
concepts.description_plain: The value a function settles towards for inputs of large magnitude is its end behaviour, and a finite value there is a horizontal asymptote.
concepts.name: Limits at infinity and horizontal asymptotes

concepts.description_formal: The limit of a quotient of two functions at infinity compares their relative magnitudes and the relative magnitudes of their rates of change.
concepts.description_plain: A quotient of two growing quantities tells which one grows faster.
concepts.name: Relative magnitude of growth compared by limits

concepts.description_formal: If f is continuous on the closed interval from a to b and d lies between f(a) and f(b), then there is at least one number c between a and b with f(c) equal to d.
concepts.description_plain: A continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values at least once.
concepts.name: The Intermediate Value Theorem
